intro: Searching for a Passivhaus architect near you usually means you want a home that is exceptionally energy-efficient, comfortable and healthy to live in, and you need someone local who understands the standard in detail. You might be planning a new build, a deep retrofit, or simply exploring what's possible. iComply introduces you to a suitable UK architect who can quote for your project directly, with fees on application.
need_heading: What people searching for a Passivhaus architect usually need
need_lead: Most people looking for a Passivhaus architect near them are at the start of a project and want to understand how to achieve the standard without compromising on design or budget.
needs: You have a plot or an existing property and want to design a home that meets the Passivhaus standard for very low energy use, comfort and air quality.
You are planning a deep retrofit of an older building and need an architect who can advise on the challenges of bringing it up to Passivhaus levels of performance.
You want to work with someone local who can visit the site regularly and collaborate with your chosen contractor and certifier.
You are unsure whether to use a certified Passivhaus designer and want to understand the difference between that and a registered architect.
You need help navigating planning permission and building regulations alongside the technical demands of airtightness and detailing.
context_heading: Understanding Passivhaus and who you're hiring
context: Passivhaus is a rigorous standard, and achieving it depends on careful design, especially when it comes to airtightness and detailing. Certified Passivhaus designers have specific training in this approach, but not all architects are certified. "Architect" is a protected title in the UK, so you can check that anyone using it is on the Architects Registration Board (ARB) register and follows the ARB code of conduct.

Many practices are also RIBA Chartered Practices, which can give you additional confidence, though architectural designers and technologists can also do excellent work—they just aren't registered architects. Before you appoint anyone, ask for a written appointment that sets out services, fees and responsibilities, and remember that building regulations approval, planning permission and party wall matters are separate processes your architect can help you navigate.

questions: Are you a certified Passivhaus designer, and can you explain your experience with the standard?
How will you approach airtightness testing and detailing to ensure we meet the standard?

faqs.q: Do I need a certified Passivhaus designer to achieve the standard?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, but certified designers have specific training in the standard and can be a valuable asset. A registered architect without certification may still have relevant experience, so ask about their track record. The key is to ensure they understand airtightness and detailing.

faqs.q: How can I check if someone is a registered architect?
faqs.a: You can check the Architects Registration Board (ARB) register online or by contacting them. Only people on the register can call themselves architects. It's also worth asking if they are a RIBA Chartered Practice.

faqs.q: What should I expect to pay for a Passivhaus architect?
faqs.a: Fees vary widely depending on the project's scope and complexity, so it's best to get a quote based on your specific needs. iComply introduces you to an architect who will quote you directly, with fees on application. You can then compare and discuss the fee proposal before appointing.
